Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $|0\rangle\in H$ be a specified unit input vector, let $A:H\to H$ be a supplied measurement-free unitary, and let $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. The access contract supplies and charges calls to $A$, its inverse $A^\dagger$, the good phase reflection
$
S_{\mathrm{good}}:=I_H-2\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},
$
and the zero-input phase reflection
$
S_0:=I_H-2|0\rangle\langle0|.
$
The signs are part of the contract: $S_{\mathrm{good}}$ is $-I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$ and $+I$ on its orthogonal complement. Reflection about the prepared state is the composite $A S_0 A^\dagger$, with its component calls charged unless a separate direct-reflection access is supplied.

Put $|\psi\rangle=A|0\rangle$ and define the initial success weight
$
a:=\|\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}|\psi\rangle\|^2\in[0,1].
$
When $a>0$, define $|G\rangle:=\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}|\psi\rangle/\sqrt a$. When $a<1$, define $|B\rangle:=(I_H-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}})|\psi\rangle/\sqrt{1-a}$. These vectors are normalized and lie respectively in the range and kernel of $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$. If $a=0$ or $a=1$, the corresponding zero component is omitted and no vector is normalized from it. With this convention,
$
|\psi\rangle=\sqrt a\,|G\rangle+\sqrt{1-a}\,|B\rangle
$
means the sum of the nonzero component terms. Under the projective measurement $\{\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},I_H-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\}$, the probability of the good outcome is $a$; the finite-dimensional rank-one density and projective-measurement outcome laws are [[thm-qc-unit-vector-projector-is-density]] and [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

The output task may return the conditional quantum state after the good outcome; that state is defined only on a positive-probability branch and is supported in $\operatorname{ran}\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$ by [[thm-qc-projective-conditional-state]]. A classical output additionally requires $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$ to be diagonal in a specified output basis and a costed coherent or ordinary verifier. An arbitrary projection does not supply a classical predicate.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. Fix the two signs

$$R_\Pi:=2\Pi-I,\qquad S_\Pi:=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi.$$

Thus $R_\Pi$ acts as $+I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and $-I$ on $\ker\Pi$; $S_\Pi$ reverses those signs. They are not interchangeable inside a controlled block. For a unit vector $\psi$, the rank-one reflection is $R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I$ with the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An access model counts a direct reflection as one primitive call only when that call is explicitly declared. Controlled reflection access is a separate declaration. If $|0\rangle$ is a specified unit input in the same space $H$, the state is prepared as $\psi=U|0\rangle$ for a declared unitary $U$, and a reflection is implemented by conjugating $R_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I$, the construction is $UR_0U^\dagger$ and its cost must include the calls to $U$, $R_0$, and $U^\dagger$. A state vector or matrix description alone implies neither an efficient reflection nor inverse access.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$\sin(z+w)=\sin z\cos w+\cos z\sin w,$$
$$\cos(z+w)=\cos z\cos w-\sin z\sin w,$$
$$\sinh(z+w)=\sinh z\cosh w+\cosh z\sinh w,$$
$$\cosh(z+w)=\cosh z\cosh w+\sinh z\sinh w.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

derivations.claim: Put $c=\sqrt{1-a}=\cos\theta$ and $s=\sqrt a=\sin\theta$. The two components $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}|\psi\rangle$ and $(I-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}})|\psi\rangle$ are orthogonal because $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$ is an orthogonal projection. Their nonzero normalized vectors therefore form an orthonormal pair, and $|\psi\rangle=c|B\rangle+s|G\rangle$. The angle $\theta$ is unique in $(0,\pi/2)$: sine is continuous there, has endpoint values $0,1$, and is strictly increasing because its derivative is the positive cosine before the first positive cosine zero.

In the ordered basis $(|B\rangle,|G\rangle)$, $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, so $S_{\mathrm{good}}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Also $A S_0 A^\dagger=I-2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$, since $A|0\rangle=|\psi\rangle$. The matrix of this latter reflection is
$
\begin{pmatrix}1-2c^2&-2cs\\-2cs&1-2s^2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-\cos(2\theta)&-\sin(2\theta)\\-\sin(2\theta)&\cos(2\theta)\end{pmatrix}.
$
The product $Q=- (A S_0 A^\dagger)S_{\mathrm{good}}$ is therefore the displayed rotation matrix. This proves invariance and the claimed restriction.

If $a=0$, then $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}|\psi\rangle=0$, so $S_{\mathrm{good}}|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle$, while $A S_0 A^\dagger|\psi\rangle=-|\psi\rangle$; hence $Q|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle$. If $a=1$, then $S_{\mathrm{good}}|\psi\rangle=-|\psi\rangle$ and $A S_0 A^\dagger|\psi\rangle=-|\psi\rangle$, hence $Q|\psi\rangle=-|\psi\rangle$. No zero component is normalized.

Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

derivations.claim: Assume $0<a<1$. The initial coordinates in the invariant ordered basis are $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. Multiplication by the matrix in [F1] and the addition formulas in [F4] send $(\cos t,\sin t)$ to $(\cos(t+2\theta),\sin(t+2\theta))$. Starting at $t=\theta$, induction on $k$ therefore gives coordinates $(\cos((2k+1)\theta),\sin((2k+1)\theta))$ after $k$ iterates.

The good component is the second coordinate, so its squared norm is $\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)$. The prepared unit vector gives a density operator by [F2], and [F3] identifies this squared component norm with the projective-measurement outcome probability.

If $a=0$, then $\theta=0$ and [F1] gives success probability $0=\sin^2((2k+1)0)$. If $a=1$, then $\theta=\pi/2$; [F1] changes only the global sign on each iterate, and [F5] gives $\sin^2((2k+1)\pi/2)=1$. Thus the same formula holds at both endpoints.

Input a coherent sampler $A$, an orthogonal success projection $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$, and a fixed integer $k\ge0$, under the access contract of [[def-qa-12-prepared-success-subspace]]. Prepare $|\psi\rangle=A|0\rangle$. In the displayed right-to-left operator convention, set
$
Q:=-A(I-2|0\rangle\langle0|)A^\dagger(I-2\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}).
$
Apply $Q$ exactly $k$ times. Then apply the projective instrument $\{\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},I-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\}$. On a positive-probability good outcome return its conditional quantum state; on the bad outcome return fail. The conditional state exists only on a positive-probability branch, as in [[thm-qc-projective-conditional-state]].

For the classical-output specialization, additionally require $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$ to be diagonal in the designated output basis and supply a costed verifier. Measure that basis only after the success-projector instrument has accepted; verify the resulting candidate and return it or fail. No arbitrary-projector-to-classical-predicate conversion is implicit.

For a $T$-query quantum algorithm [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] at input length $n$, its **worst-case quantum query cost** is the maximum number of designated oracle calls over all promised instances in $P_n$ and all measurement branches. When $P_n$ is empty, define this cost to be $0$. For nonempty $P_n$, a finite circuit and finite branch sets ensure that this maximum exists; a solver whose branch counts are not uniformly bounded has infinite worst-case query cost. An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

In the pure query model, ordinary gates outside the oracle calls are uncharged by the query coordinate. If a task also reports gate, preparation, measurement, or classical costs, those are separate coordinates. Bounded-error query cost uses the same worst-case maximum; its success threshold is the per-instance condition in [[def-qa-bounded-error-promise-correctness]], not an average over oracle inputs.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, $w(C)$ its total number of wires, and $a_{\rm clean}(C),a_{\rm dirty}(C)$ the numbers of wires that satisfy the exact clean and dirty ancilla contracts of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. Auxiliary wires that satisfy neither contract are still counted in $w(C)$ and are not silently included in either ancilla count ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

derivations.claim: The initial preparation in [F1] contributes one forward $A$ call. No inverse call occurs before the iterates.

Each of the $k$ displayed $Q$-factors contains exactly one $A$, one $A^\dagger$, one $S_0$, and one $S_{\mathrm{good}}$. Adding these to the initial preparation gives $k+1$ forward $A$ calls, $k$ inverse $A^\dagger$ calls, and $k$ of each phase operation. The final instrument is not an oracle call unless the chosen model explicitly assigns it one.

By [F2]–[F3], any verifier, controlled access, gate synthesis, state-preparation construction, and classical postprocessing retains its own declared charge; none changes the factor counts in step 1.2.

Input a coherent sampler with an exactly represented known success weight $a\in[0,1]$. For the finite rational-input procedure, $a$ is given as a binary rational; exact algebraic inputs are also allowed when the supplied representation supports exact comparisons. If $a=0$, return fail without normalizing a good component. If $a=1$, prepare $A|0\rangle$, apply the declared good/bad projective instrument, and return its good conditional state (or, in the diagonal classical-output specialization, measure and verify the output).

For $0<a<1$, set $\theta:=\arcsin\sqrt a\in(0,\pi/2)$, using the principal inverse-sine and nonnegative-square-root conventions of [[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]] and [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Then $\theta$ is the unique angle with $\sin^2\theta=a$. Set $K:=\lceil1/\sqrt a\rceil$, equivalently the least positive integer $K$ with $K^2a\ge1$. For each integer $k=0,\ldots,K$, compute $p_k=\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)$ exactly by the rational recurrence
$
x_0=1,\qquad x_1=1-2a,\qquad x_{n+1}=2(1-2a)x_n-x_{n-1}\ (n\ge1),\qquad p_k=(1-x_{2k+1})/2.
$
Indeed, writing $x_n=\cos(2n\theta)$, double-angle gives $x_0=1$, $x_1=\cos(2\theta)=1-2a$, and cosine addition gives the displayed recurrence. Also $\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)=(1-\cos((4k+2)\theta))/2=(1-x_{2k+1})/2$. Choose the least $k$ attaining the maximum of this finite list. Run the fixed-$k$ procedure [[alg-qa-12-amplitude-amplification]], verify when a classical candidate is requested, and return the good conditional output or fail. For rational $a$, every $x_n$ and $p_k$ is rational, so the comparisons are exact. No time bound for this classical preprocessing is claimed.

Let $a\in[0,1]$ be the initial success weight and let $\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ be the unique angle satisfying $\sin^2\theta=a$. After exactly $k\ge0$ standard amplitude-amplification iterates, the probability of the good outcome of $\{\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},I-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\}$ is
$
\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).
$
The endpoints $a=0$ and $a=1$ are included by direct evaluation, without normalizing a zero component.

$$\tan(\pi-x)=-\tan x,\quad \cot(\pi-x)=-\cot x,\quad \sec(\pi-x)=-\sec x,\quad \csc(\pi-x)=\csc x.$$

$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: If $1/2\le a<1$, the candidate $k=0$ belongs to the finite search range and has success probability $\sin^2\theta=a=\max\{a,1-a\}$ by [F2]. The maximizing $k$ therefore has at least this probability.

Suppose $0<a<1/2$. Let $s=\sin(\pi/4)=\cos(\pi/4)>0$, where positivity follows from strict increase in [F5]. By [F6], $1=\sin(\pi/2)=2s^2$, so $s=1/\sqrt2$. Since $\sin\theta=\sqrt a<1/\sqrt2=s$, [F5] gives $0<\theta<\pi/4$. Put $r=\pi/(4\theta)-1/2>0$, and choose a nearest nonnegative integer $k_0$ to $r$, breaking ties toward the smaller integer. Then $|k_0-r|\le1/2$, so $|(2k_0+1)\theta-\pi/2|\le\theta$. The addition and Pythagorean identities [F3] give $\sin^2((2k_0+1)\theta)\ge\cos^2\theta=1-a$.

Since $\sin\theta=\sqrt a$, [F4] gives $\theta\ge\sqrt a$. Hence $k_0\le r+1/2=\pi/(4\theta)\le\pi/(4\sqrt a)<1/\sqrt a$ by [F7], so $k_0\le\lceil1/\sqrt a\rceil$. Thus $k_0$ lies in the algorithm's finite range, and [F1]–[F2] show that its selected maximizer has probability at least $1-a=\max\{a,1-a\}$. The explicit zero and unit-weight branches give the stated endpoint behavior.

A halted history is extended by deterministic idle steps that issue no calls.

$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

For every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\frac1{1+x^2},\qquad \arctan x=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}.$$

For $|x|<1$,

$$\arctan x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}.$$

At the endpoint, the ordinarily convergent alternating series satisfies

$$\frac\pi4=1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\cdots.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(\pi/2-x)=\cos x,\quad \cos(\pi/2-x)=\sin x,\quad \sin(\pi-x)=\sin x,\quad \cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x,$$
and the quarter-turn and reflection formulas are
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad \cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad \sin(-x)=-\sin x,\quad \cos(-x)=\cos x.$$
On the common natural domains of the two sides,
$$\tan(\pi/2-x)=\cot x,\quad \cot(\pi/2-x)=\tan x,\quad \sec(\pi/2-x)=\csc x,\quad \csc(\pi/2-x)=\sec x,$$
and
$$\tan(\pi-x)=-\tan x,\quad \cot(\pi-x)=-\cot x,\quad \sec(\pi-x)=-\sec x,\quad \csc(\pi-x)=\csc x.$$
The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].
$\sin\pi=0$, and $\sin x>0$ for every $x$ with $0<x<\pi$. Thus $\pi$ is the first positive zero of sine.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

derivations.claim:
In the ordered $(|G\rangle,|B\rangle)$ basis, set $u=e^{i\phi}$ and $v=e^{i\varphi}$. Since $|u|=|v|=1$ by [F5], the phase operations act by unit-modulus scalars on orthogonal subspaces and are unitary. From $A|0\rangle=|\psi\rangle$ and the supplied phase operators, the iterate has matrix
$$Q=-\begin{pmatrix} v((1-a)+au)&(u-1)\sqrt{a(1-a)}\\ v(u-1)\sqrt{a(1-a)}&a+(1-a)u \end{pmatrix}.$$
The diagonal entries coincide by [F1]. The common diagonal is nonzero because the imaginary part of $(1-a)+ae^{i\phi}$ is $a\sin\phi>0$. The lower-left entry has modulus $2\sin(\phi/2)\sqrt{a(1-a)}=\sin(\phi/2)\sin(2\theta)=\sin\vartheta$. Thus the matched and implemented iterates are unitary and the matched matrix has equal diagonal entries.

Write the common diagonal as $d$ and the lower-left entry as $c$. Unitarity gives $|d|^2+|c|^2=1$, so $|d|=\cos\vartheta$ because $|c|=\sin\vartheta$ and $\vartheta\in(0,\pi/2]$. Since $d,c\ne0$, put $\eta=d/|d|$ and $\zeta=(c/|c|)\overline\eta$; both have modulus one, and $d=\eta\cos\vartheta$, $c=\eta\zeta\sin\vartheta$. If $b$ is the upper-right entry, column orthogonality $\overline d\,b+\overline c\,d=0$ gives $b=-\eta\overline\zeta\sin\vartheta$. Hence $Q=\eta D R(\vartheta)D^{-1}$, with $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\zeta)$ and $R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$.

Write $m\vartheta=\pi/2+t$. From $m=\lceil\pi/(2\vartheta)-1/2\rceil$ we get $|t|\le\vartheta/2$. Quarter-turn, parity, and monotonicity identities give $\sin(m\vartheta)=\cos t\ge\cos(\vartheta/2)$ and $|\cos(m\vartheta)|=|\sin t|\le\sin(\vartheta/2)$. If $a\ge1/4$, failure is at most $1\le4a$. If $a<1/4$, put $c=\cos(\pi/3)=\sin(\pi/6)$ by [F13]. Since $0<\pi/6<\pi$, [F13] gives $c>0$, while the double-angle and supplementary identities give $2c^2-1=\cos(2\pi/3)=-c$. Thus $(2c-1)(c+1)=0$, and positivity yields $c=1/2$. Hence $\sin\theta=\sqrt a<\sin(\pi/6)$, so $\theta<\pi/6$ by [F14]. Because $\sin\vartheta=\sin(\phi/2)\sin(2\theta)\le\sin(2\theta)$ and both angles lie in $[0,\pi/2]$, [F14] gives $\vartheta\le2\theta$. The addition formulas [F9] and induction give $R(\vartheta)^m=R(m\vartheta)$. The initial coordinates are $(\sqrt a,\sqrt{1-a})$, so the first coordinate of $\eta^mD R(m\vartheta)D^{-1}(\sqrt a,\sqrt{1-a})$ has modulus
$$\left|\sqrt a\cos(m\vartheta)-\overline\zeta\sqrt{1-a}\sin(m\vartheta)\right| \ge\sqrt{1-a}|\sin(m\vartheta)|-\sqrt a|\cos(m\vartheta)| \ge\sqrt{1-a}\cos(\vartheta/2)-\sqrt a\sin(\vartheta/2) \ge(1-a)-a=1-2a.$$
The last inequality uses $\vartheta/2\le\theta$, cosine decreasing and sine increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$, and $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-a}$, $\sin\theta=\sqrt a$. The scalar $\eta^m$ has modulus one and $D$ leaves the good coordinate unchanged. By [F7], the matched failure probability is therefore at most $1-(1-2a)^2\le4a$.

Let $Q'$ be the iterate with phase $\varphi'$. The arbitrary-phase definition gives
$$Q'-Q=-A S_0(\phi)A^\dagger(e^{i\varphi'}-e^{i\varphi})\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}.$$
For every unit vector $x$, the projection contraction in [F6] and unitarity give $\|(Q'-Q)x\|\le|e^{i\varphi'}-e^{i\varphi}|\le\delta$ by [F5], hence $\|Q'-Q\|\le\delta$. Telescoping yields
$$Q'^m-Q^m=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}Q'^{\,m-1-r}(Q'-Q)Q^r,$$
so unitarity gives $\|Q'^m-Q^m\|\le m\delta$. Set $x=Q^m|\psi\rangle$ and $y=Q'^m|\psi\rangle$ for $|\psi\rangle=A|0\rangle$. Then $\|x-y\|\le\|Q'^m-Q^m\|\le m\delta$. By [F7], the failure probabilities are $\|\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}x\|^2$ and $\|\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}y\|^2$. Contraction of $\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}$ and reverse triangle give
$$\left|\|\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}x\|^2-\|\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}y\|^2\right| \le(\|\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}x\|+\|\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}y\|)\|x-y\| \le2\|x-y\|\le2m\delta.$$
Thus implemented failure is at most $4a+2m\delta$ by step 3.1.

For $a<1/4$, $\sin(2\theta)=2\sqrt{a(1-a)}\ge\sqrt3\sqrt a$. Set $x=\phi/2\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $g(x)=\sin x-2x/\pi$. By [F8], [F15], $g(0)=g(\pi/2)=0$; by [F14], $g''(x)=-\sin x\le0$. The derivatives in [F8], [F11] make $g'$ differentiable, hence continuous by [F16]; the mean value theorem [F10] applied to $g'$ gives $g'(t)\le g'(s)$ for $0\le s<t\le\pi/2$. The same facts make $g$ continuous and differentiable, so [F10] on $[0,x]$ and $[x,\pi/2]$ gives slopes $g(x)/x$ and $-g(x)/(\pi/2-x)$; the first is at least the second, so $g(x)\ge0$. Therefore $\sin(\phi/2)\ge\phi/\pi$, $\sin\vartheta\ge\sqrt3\phi\sqrt a/\pi$, and $\vartheta\ge\sin\vartheta$ by [F5], [F8]. Also $1=\sin(\pi/2)\le\pi/2$ by [F5], [F8], so $1/(2\pi)\le1$. The ceiling gives
$$m\le\frac{\pi}{2\vartheta}+\frac12 \le\frac{\pi^2}{2\sqrt3\,\phi\sqrt a}+\frac12 \le\frac{\pi(\pi+\sqrt3)}{2\sqrt3\,\phi\sqrt a},$$
where the last inequality uses $\phi\sqrt a\le\pi$. Under $\delta\le C\epsilon\phi\sqrt a$ with $C=\sqrt3/(2\pi^2(\sqrt3+\pi))$, we obtain $2m\delta\le\epsilon/(2\pi)\le\epsilon$. Step 4.1 gives failure at most $4a+\epsilon$; when $a\ge1/4$, the same bound is automatic since failure is at most $1\le4a$.

In the equal-phase case with $a\le1/4$, put $T=\tan(\phi/2)>0$ and $r=1-2a\in[1/2,1]$. The matching condition [F1] and the principal inverse tangent [F12] give $\varphi=2\arctan(rT)$ and $\delta=2(\arctan T-\arctan(rT))$. Let $f(s)=\arctan(sT)$. By [F11], [F12], $f''(s)=-2sT^3/(1+s^2T^2)^2\le0$; differentiability and [F16] give the continuity needed to apply [F10] to $f'$, so $f'$ is nonincreasing. Applying [F10] to $f$ on $[0,r]$ and $[r,1]$, the early secant slope is at least the late one; the secant slope on $[0,1]$, their weighted average, is therefore at least the late slope. Thus $f(1)-f(r)\le(1-r)(f(1)-f(0))\le(1-r)\pi/2$, so $\delta\le\pi(1-r)=2\pi a$. If $\delta>0$, apply step 4.1 with $\epsilon=\delta/(C\phi\sqrt a)$; if $\delta=0$, step 3.1 gives the matched bound. The resulting failure is at most $4a+(2\pi/C)\sqrt a/\phi\le(4\pi+2\pi/C)\sqrt a/\phi$. For $a\ge1/4$, $1\le2\pi\sqrt a/\phi$, so the same big-O bound holds on the full range.

Input a prepared sampler $A$, a success projection $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$, an integer $m\ge0$, and phases $\phi,\varphi\in[0,2\pi)$. In addition to $A,A^\dagger$, the access contract must supply the exact phase operations
$
S_0(\phi)=I+(e^{i\phi}-1)|0\rangle\langle0|,\qquad
S_{\mathrm{good}}(\varphi)=I+(e^{i\varphi}-1)\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},
$
and charge each call. Such access does not follow from a $\pi$-phase reflection alone. Prepare $A|0\rangle$, apply
$
Q(\phi,\varphi):=-A S_0(\phi)A^\dagger S_{\mathrm{good}}(\varphi)
$
exactly $m$ times, and apply the declared good/bad projective instrument. Return the conditional quantum output on a positive-probability good branch or fail on the bad branch. A classical output additionally needs the diagonal-predicate and costed-verifier conditions in [[def-qa-12-prepared-success-subspace]].

For a finite-dimensional unitary $U$, **inverse access** is the explicitly granted operation $U^\dagger=U^{-1}$. Its availability and query or gate charge are recorded separately from forward access, including any controlled access in [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. For a chronological sequence of length $k\ge0$ that applies $U_1$ first and $U_k$ last, the total operator is $W=U_k\cdots U_1$ when $k>0$ and $W=I_H$ when $k=0$. For $k>0$, the inverse sequence applies $U_k^\dagger$ first, then $U_{k-1}^\dagger$, down to $U_1^\dagger$; for $k=0$ it is the empty sequence.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, $w(C)$ its total number of wires, and $a_{\rm clean}(C),a_{\rm dirty}(C)$ the numbers of wires that satisfy the exact clean and dirty ancilla contracts of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. Auxiliary wires that satisfy neither contract are still counted in $w(C)$ and are not silently included in either ancilla count ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

For a $T$-query quantum algorithm [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] at input length $n$, its **worst-case quantum query cost** is the maximum number of designated oracle calls over all promised instances in $P_n$ and all measurement branches. When $P_n$ is empty, define this cost to be $0$. For nonempty $P_n$, a finite circuit and finite branch sets ensure that this maximum exists; a solver whose branch counts are not uniformly bounded has infinite worst-case query cost. An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

In the pure query model, ordinary gates outside the oracle calls are uncharged by the query coordinate. If a task also reports gate, preparation, measurement, or classical costs, those are separate coordinates. Bounded-error query cost uses the same worst-case maximum; its success threshold is the per-instance condition in [[def-qa-bounded-error-promise-correctness]], not an average over oracle inputs.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and $U:H\to H$ a unitary. Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, and suppose the model separately grants controlled access to both $U$ and $e^{i\theta}U$. There is a normalized eigenvector $\phi$ with $U\phi=\mu\phi$ and $|\mu|=1$. Let $C=Q_2=\mathbb C^2$ be the control qubit with ordered computational basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$; define $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and prepare $(|0\rangle+\overline\mu|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ with target $\phi$. The two joint effects are $E_\pm=|\pm\rangle\langle\pm|\otimes I_H$. The $E_+$ outcome has probability $1$ after $C(U)$ and $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ after $C(e^{i\theta}U)$. Thus the two controlled maps give different outcome laws exactly when $\theta\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$; when $\theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the controlled maps coincide. This is a mathematical witness; it does not assert that controlled access or the witness-state preparation is free.

derivations.claim: The initial preparation in [F1] uses one forward call to $A$. Each of the $m$ factors of $Q$ contributes exactly one $A$, one $A^\dagger$, one $S_0(\phi)$, and one $S_{\mathrm{good}}(\varphi)$, giving the stated counts. The projective instrument and optional verifier occur once after the loop.

The access and cost conventions in [F3]–[F4] keep any controlled access, phase-gate synthesis, state preparation, and verification in their own coordinates. In particular, replacing $Q$ by $-Q$ inside a controlled call changes the relative control phase and is not a free rewrite.

Input a coherent sampler $A$, an orthogonal success projection $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$, and a fixed integer $k\ge0$, under the access contract of [[def-qa-12-prepared-success-subspace]]. Prepare $|\psi\rangle=A|0\rangle$. In the displayed right-to-left operator convention, set
$
Q:=-A(I-2|0\rangle\langle0|)A^\dagger(I-2\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}).
$
Apply $Q$ exactly $k$ times. Then apply the projective instrument $\{\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},I-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\}$. On a positive-probability good outcome return its conditional quantum state; on the bad outcome return fail. The conditional state exists only on a positive-probability branch, as in [[thm-qc-projective-conditional-state]].

For the classical-output specialization, additionally require $\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}$ to be diagonal in the designated output basis and supply a costed verifier. Measure that basis only after the success-projector instrument has accepted; verify the resulting candidate and return it or fail. No arbitrary-projector-to-classical-predicate conversion is implicit.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. Fix the two signs

$$R_\Pi:=2\Pi-I,\qquad S_\Pi:=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi.$$

Thus $R_\Pi$ acts as $+I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and $-I$ on $\ker\Pi$; $S_\Pi$ reverses those signs. They are not interchangeable inside a controlled block. For a unit vector $\psi$, the rank-one reflection is $R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I$ with the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An access model counts a direct reflection as one primitive call only when that call is explicitly declared. Controlled reflection access is a separate declaration. If $|0\rangle$ is a specified unit input in the same space $H$, the state is prepared as $\psi=U|0\rangle$ for a declared unitary $U$, and a reflection is implemented by conjugating $R_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I$, the construction is $UR_0U^\dagger$ and its cost must include the calls to $U$, $R_0$, and $U^\dagger$. A state vector or matrix description alone implies neither an efficient reflection nor inverse access.

For a finite-dimensional unitary $U$, **inverse access** is the explicitly granted operation $U^\dagger=U^{-1}$. Its availability and query or gate charge are recorded separately from forward access, including any controlled access in [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. For a chronological sequence of length $k\ge0$ that applies $U_1$ first and $U_k$ last, the total operator is $W=U_k\cdots U_1$ when $k>0$ and $W=I_H$ when $k=0$. For $k>0$, the inverse sequence applies $U_k^\dagger$ first, then $U_{k-1}^\dagger$, down to $U_1^\dagger$; for $k=0$ it is the empty sequence.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. $$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

For a $T$-query quantum algorithm [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] at input length $n$, its **worst-case quantum query cost** is the maximum number of designated oracle calls over all promised instances in $P_n$ and all measurement branches. When $P_n$ is empty, define this cost to be $0$. An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

In the pure query model, ordinary gates outside the oracle calls are uncharged by the query coordinate. If a task also reports gate, preparation, measurement, or classical costs, those are separate coordinates. Bounded-error query cost uses the same worst-case maximum; its success threshold is the per-instance condition in [[def-qa-bounded-error-promise-correctness]], not an average over oracle inputs.

$
\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).
$
The endpoints $a=0$ and $a=1$ are included by direct evaluation, without normalizing a zero component.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(\pi/2-x)=\cos x,\quad \cos(\pi/2-x)=\sin x,\quad \sin(\pi-x)=\sin x,\quad \cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x,$$
and the quarter-turn and reflection formulas are
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad \cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad \sin(-x)=-\sin x,\quad \cos(-x)=\cos x.$$
On the common natural domains of the two sides,
$$\tan(\pi/2-x)=\cot x,\quad \cot(\pi/2-x)=\tan x,\quad \sec(\pi/2-x)=\csc x,\quad \csc(\pi/2-x)=\sec x,$$
and
$$\tan(\pi-x)=-\tan x,\quad \cot(\pi-x)=-\cot x,\quad \sec(\pi-x)=-\sec x,\quad \csc(\pi-x)=\csc x.$$
The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].
